## Summary

We asked whether information known before a Himalayan expedition sets off can predict whether an individual climber will reach the summit. Using 59,904 member records from 8,420 expeditions in the Nepal Himalaya between 1990 and 2019, taken from the Himalayan Database, we compared a logistic regression model with a gradient boosting model. We split the data by expedition and evaluated the models with balanced accuracy, so that both outcomes count equally. Gradient boosting performed best, with a balanced accuracy of 0.71 on expeditions it had never seen, compared with 0.50 for a baseline that ignores the predictors. Expedition role, hired status and supplemental oxygen use were among the features most strongly linked to success. These results show that planning factors carry real information about who reaches the summit, but much of the outcome depends on conditions that cannot be known in advance, so the predictions are uncertain for any single climber. The main limitations are that the expedition oxygen indicator may be partly recorded after the climb (without it, logistic regression dropped from 0.68 to 0.65), that some roles partly reveal whether a member intended to summit, that the data end in 2019, and that a few popular peaks dominate the data.

## Introduction

Climbing in the Nepal Himalaya has grown into a commercial industry. Guided expeditions now take paying clients up some of the highest mountains in the world, supported by hired guides and high-altitude workers, many of whom are Sherpa. The risks of this work are serious and unevenly shared: about one third of all deaths on Everest have been Sherpa climbers (Preiss 2018). Climbers, the agencies that organise expeditions and the authorities that issue climbing permits all make important decisions before an expedition sets off, such as which peak to attempt, in which season, with how large a team and with how much hired support. Knowing how strongly these choices are linked to reaching the summit could help climbers set realistic expectations and help organisers plan their expeditions.

In this project we ask whether information known before an expedition begins can predict whether an individual climber will reach the summit. We treat this as a binary classification problem in which each observation is one expedition member and the target is whether that member summited. The predictors describe the climber (age, sex, citizenship, role on the team and whether they were hired staff), the expedition (year, season, team size, number of hired staff and whether the expedition used supplemental oxygen) and the peak (its height). We use the Himalayan Database (Hawley and Salisbury 2020), which records expeditions to more than 465 peaks in the Nepal Himalaya from 1905 to spring 2019, in the version prepared for the TidyTuesday project (TidyTuesday 2020).

## Methods

### Data

The code below downloads the three tables used in this analysis (one row per expedition member, one per expedition and one per peak) from the TidyTuesday repository and saves unmodified copies to the raw data folder before any processing.

```{python}
import os
import urllib.request

# Source: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2020/2020-09-22
BASE_URL = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/"
    "main/data/2020/2020-09-22/"
)
RAW_DIR = "../data/raw"
os.makedirs(RAW_DIR, exist_ok=True)

for name in ["members", "expeditions", "peaks"]:
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{BASE_URL}{name}.csv", f"{RAW_DIR}/{name}.csv")
```

Each observation in our analysis is one expedition member, and the target is whether that member reached the summit. We joined each member to their expedition's team size, number of hired staff and whether the expedition used supplemental oxygen, and to the height of the peak attempted. We kept only information that would be known before the climb begins. We removed every variable recorded during or after the expedition: the highest point the member reached, whether they died or were injured, and the cause and altitude of any death or injury. We also removed the member-level indicator of oxygen use, because a climber who turns back early never reaches the altitude where oxygen is used, so this variable partly records the outcome. We used the expedition-level indicator instead, as an approximation of planned oxygen use.

We restricted the data to expeditions from 1990 onward, to focus on the modern era of commercial climbing, and removed one record with an unknown season. The final data set contains 59,904 member records from 8,420 expeditions on 325 peaks.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

members = pd.read_csv(f"{RAW_DIR}/members.csv")
expeditions = pd.read_csv(f"{RAW_DIR}/expeditions.csv")
peaks = pd.read_csv(f"{RAW_DIR}/peaks.csv")

# Columns recorded during or after the climb. These reveal the outcome.
LEAKY_MEMBER_COLS = [
    "highpoint_metres", "died", "death_cause", "death_height_metres",
    "injured", "injury_type", "injury_height_metres",
    "oxygen_used",  # whether this member actually used oxygen
]

expedition_info = (
    expeditions[["expedition_id", "year", "members", "hired_staff", "oxygen_used"]]
    .rename(columns={"members": "team_size", "oxygen_used": "expedition_oxygen"})
)
peak_info = peaks[["peak_id", "height_metres"]].rename(
    columns={"height_metres": "peak_height_m"}
)

himalaya = (
    members
    .drop(columns=LEAKY_MEMBER_COLS)
    .drop_duplicates(subset=["expedition_id", "member_id"])
    .merge(expedition_info, on=["expedition_id", "year"], how="left", validate="many_to_one")
    .merge(peak_info, on="peak_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
    .query("year >= 1990 and season != 'Unknown'")
)

FEATURES = [
    "year", "season", "sex", "age", "citizenship", "expedition_role",
    "hired", "solo", "team_size", "hired_staff", "expedition_oxygen",
    "peak_height_m",
]
TARGET = "success"

himalaya = himalaya[["expedition_id", "peak_name"] + FEATURES + [TARGET]]

PROCESSED_DIR = "../data/processed"
os.makedirs(PROCESSED_DIR, exist_ok=True)
himalaya.to_csv(f"{PROCESSED_DIR}/himalaya_clean.csv", index=False)
```

Members of the same expedition share a team, a route, weather and a leader, so their outcomes are strongly related. If members of one expedition appeared in both the training and test sets, the model could partly memorise expedition-level conditions, and its test performance would overstate how well it predicts for a new expedition. We therefore split the data by expedition rather than by individual. 70% of expeditions went to the training set (42,446 members from 5,894 expeditions) and 30% to the test set (17,458 members from 2,526 expeditions), so that no expedition appears in both. Missing values and rare categories are handled inside the modelling pipeline using the training data only, as described in the next section.

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit

splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.3, random_state=522)
train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(himalaya, groups=himalaya["expedition_id"]))
train_df = himalaya.iloc[train_idx]
test_df = himalaya.iloc[test_idx]

# No expedition should appear in both sets
assert set(train_df["expedition_id"]).isdisjoint(test_df["expedition_id"])

train_df.to_csv(f"{PROCESSED_DIR}/himalaya_train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv(f"{PROCESSED_DIR}/himalaya_test.csv", index=False)
```

### Exploratory data analysis

We explored the training set only, so that nothing about the test set influenced our choices of features, preprocessing or evaluation metric. We made the figures with Altair (VanderPlas et al. 2018) and computed the distributions with NumPy (Harris et al. 2020).

```{python}
import altair as alt
import numpy as np

OUTCOME_LABELS = {True: "Summited", False: "Did not summit"}
OUTCOME_SCALE = alt.Scale(
    domain=["Summited", "Did not summit"], range=["#1b9e77", "#d95f02"]
)

overall_rate = train_df["success"].mean()
majority_rate = 1 - overall_rate
n_train = len(train_df)

overall_pct = f"{overall_rate:.0%}"
majority_pct = f"{majority_rate:.0%}"
n_train_str = f"{n_train:,}"
```

Of the `{python} n_train_str` members in the training set, `{python} overall_pct` reached the summit (@fig-class-balance). The classes are moderately imbalanced: a model that always predicted "did not summit" would be correct `{python} majority_pct` of the time without learning anything. Plain accuracy would therefore make such a model look better than it is. We have no strong reason to treat one kind of error as worse than the other, since wrongly predicting success and wrongly predicting failure are both misleading to a climber or an organiser. We therefore evaluate models with balanced accuracy, the average of the proportion of summiters and the proportion of non-summiters that a model classifies correctly. A model that ignores either class scores no better than 50%.

```{python}
#| label: fig-class-balance
#| fig-cap: "Number of members in the training set who did and did not reach the summit."
balance = (
    train_df["success"]
    .map(OUTCOME_LABELS)
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("outcome")
    .reset_index(name="members")
)

alt.Chart(balance).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X("members:Q", title="Number of members"),
    y=alt.Y("outcome:N", title=None, sort="-x"),
    color=alt.Color("outcome:N", scale=OUTCOME_SCALE, legend=None),
    tooltip=["outcome", "members"],
).properties(width=450, height=80)
```

@fig-categorical shows the success rate for each level of the main categorical features, with the overall success rate as a dashed line. Being hired staff is the strongest single signal: hired staff summited about twice as often as other members, which makes sense because many of them are guides who accompany clients to the top. Members of expeditions that used supplemental oxygen also summited far more often. This is partly because oxygen is used mainly on the highest and most commercial peaks, and partly because the expedition-level oxygen indicator may itself be partly recorded after the climb, a limitation we return to in the Discussion. Spring was the most successful season and autumn the second. Winter and summer had lower success rates, but very few members climbed in those seasons, so their rates are less certain. Men summited somewhat more often than women, although women made up only about one in ten members. Solo climbs are too rare (58 members) to show here.

```{python}
#| label: fig-categorical
#| fig-cap: "Success rate in the training set by season, hired status, expedition oxygen use and sex. The dashed line is the overall success rate."
YES_NO = {True: "Yes", False: "No"}
SEX_LABELS = {"M": "Male", "F": "Female"}


def success_rate_chart(column, title, labels=None):
    rates = (
        train_df.groupby(column)["success"]
        .agg(rate="mean", members="size")
        .reset_index()
    )
    if labels is not None:
        rates[column] = rates[column].map(labels)
    bars = alt.Chart(rates).mark_bar(color="#7570b3").encode(
        x=alt.X(f"{column}:N", title=title, sort="-y", axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
        y=alt.Y(
            "rate:Q",
            title="Success rate",
            scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1]),
            axis=alt.Axis(format="%"),
        ),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip(f"{column}:N", title=title),
            alt.Tooltip("rate:Q", title="Success rate", format=".1%"),
            alt.Tooltip("members:Q", title="Members", format=","),
        ],
    )
    overall = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({"rate": [overall_rate]})).mark_rule(
        strokeDash=[4, 4], color="black"
    ).encode(y="rate:Q")
    return (bars + overall).properties(width=180, height=180)


(
    success_rate_chart("season", "Season")
    | success_rate_chart("hired", "Hired staff", YES_NO)
) & (
    success_rate_chart("expedition_oxygen", "Expedition used oxygen", YES_NO)
    | success_rate_chart("sex", "Sex", SEX_LABELS)
)
```

@fig-numeric compares the distributions of the numeric features for members who did and did not summit. Members who summited were slightly younger and tended to come from more recent years, which is consistent with success rates rising as commercial climbing became more organised. Their expeditions also had more hired staff. In contrast, the distributions of peak height and team size overlap almost completely, so on their own these features separate the two outcomes poorly. We still keep them as predictors, because they may matter in combination with other features. For example, the effect of hired support or oxygen may depend on how high the peak is.

```{python}
#| label: fig-numeric
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of the numeric features in the training set for members who did and did not reach the summit. Each distribution is scaled to have area one. For team size and hired staff, the largest 1% of values are not shown so that the rest of the distribution is visible."
NUMERIC_TITLES = {
    "age": "Age (years)",
    "year": "Year",
    "peak_height_m": "Peak height (m)",
    "team_size": "Team size",
    "hired_staff": "Number of hired staff",
}
CLIP_TOP = ["team_size", "hired_staff"]


def distribution_chart(column, bins=25):
    values = train_df[column].dropna()
    upper = values.quantile(0.99) if column in CLIP_TOP else values.max()
    edges = np.histogram_bin_edges(values, bins=bins, range=(values.min(), upper))
    frames = []
    for outcome, group in train_df.groupby("success"):
        density, _ = np.histogram(group[column].dropna(), bins=edges, density=True)
        frames.append(
            pd.DataFrame(
                {
                    "value": (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2,
                    "density": density,
                    "outcome": OUTCOME_LABELS[outcome],
                }
            )
        )
    return (
        alt.Chart(pd.concat(frames))
        .mark_area(opacity=0.5, interpolate="monotone")
        .encode(
            x=alt.X(
                "value:Q",
                title=NUMERIC_TITLES[column],
                scale=alt.Scale(zero=False),
                axis=alt.Axis(format="d") if column == "year" else alt.Axis(),
            ),
            y=alt.Y("density:Q", title="Density", stack=None),
            color=alt.Color("outcome:N", scale=OUTCOME_SCALE, title="Outcome"),
        )
        .properties(width=200, height=150)
    )


alt.concat(
    *[distribution_chart(c) for c in NUMERIC_TITLES], columns=3
).configure_legend(orient="top")
```

Finally, @fig-peaks shows that the data are dominated by a few popular peaks. Everest alone accounts for about 31% of the training members, and Everest, Cho Oyu and Ama Dablam together account for about 58%. Success rates also differ widely between peaks of almost the same height. Manaslu (8,163 m) and Dhaulagiri I (8,167 m) are only 4 metres apart, yet about 43% of members summited Manaslu compared with about 24% on Dhaulagiri I. Himlung Himal and Pumori, both just over 7,100 m, show a similar gap (about 41% and 28%). This suggests that the route and level of commercial support on a peak matter, not just its height. Because peak identity is not one of our predictors, the model can capture these differences only through peak height and the other features. It may also perform best on the most frequently climbed peaks, since they make up most of the data it learns from.

```{python}
#| label: fig-peaks
#| fig-cap: "The ten peaks with the most members in the training set: number of members (left) and success rate (right). The dashed line is the overall success rate."
top_peaks = train_df["peak_name"].value_counts().head(10).index
peak_summary = (
    train_df[train_df["peak_name"].isin(top_peaks)]
    .groupby("peak_name")["success"]
    .agg(members="size", rate="mean")
    .reset_index()
)
peak_order = alt.EncodingSortField(field="members", order="descending")

peak_counts = alt.Chart(peak_summary).mark_bar(color="#7570b3").encode(
    x=alt.X("members:Q", title="Number of members"),
    y=alt.Y("peak_name:N", title=None, sort=peak_order),
    tooltip=["peak_name", alt.Tooltip("members:Q", format=",")],
)
peak_rates = alt.Chart(peak_summary).mark_bar(color="#7570b3").encode(
    x=alt.X(
        "rate:Q",
        title="Success rate",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1]),
        axis=alt.Axis(format="%"),
    ),
    y=alt.Y("peak_name:N", title=None, sort=peak_order, axis=None),
    tooltip=["peak_name", alt.Tooltip("rate:Q", format=".1%")],
)
peak_overall = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({"rate": [overall_rate]})).mark_rule(
    strokeDash=[4, 4], color="black"
).encode(x="rate:Q")

(
    peak_counts.properties(width=250, height=250)
    | (peak_rates + peak_overall).properties(width=200, height=250)
)
```

### Modelling

We used twelve predictors: five numeric features (year, age, team size, number of hired staff and peak height), four categorical features (season, sex, citizenship and expedition role) and three binary features (whether the member was hired staff, whether they climbed solo and whether the expedition used supplemental oxygen). The expedition identifier and peak name were not used as predictors.

All preprocessing was done inside a scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011) pipeline, so that during cross-validation (CV) each step was fitted only on the training folds and nothing was learned from the fold being scored. Numeric features were imputed with the median, because age is missing for about 3% of training members and its distribution is slightly right-skewed, and then standardised so that their scales are comparable. Missing citizenship and expedition role values were replaced with an "Unknown" level. Citizenship has close to 200 levels and expedition role more than 250, most of them very rare. Rather than choosing the levels to keep by hand, we one-hot encoded these features and grouped every level seen fewer than 100 times in the training data into a single "infrequent" level. This keeps the common countries and roles while preventing the model from fitting noise in levels with only a handful of members. The binary features were encoded as a single indicator each.

Because members of the same expedition share conditions that strongly affect their outcomes, we used grouped 5-fold cross-validation with the expedition as the group, for the same reason that we split the training and test sets by expedition. Every model was evaluated with balanced accuracy, as justified in the exploratory analysis. Because the expedition oxygen indicator may be partly recorded after the climb, we also refitted the logistic regression without it, to measure how much the model relies on this feature.

```{python}
from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

NUMERIC = ["year", "age", "team_size", "hired_staff", "peak_height_m"]
CATEGORICAL = ["season", "sex", "citizenship", "expedition_role"]
BINARY = ["hired", "solo", "expedition_oxygen"]
MIN_CATEGORY_COUNT = 100

X_train = train_df[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL + BINARY]
y_train = train_df["success"]
groups_train = train_df["expedition_id"]
cv = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)


def make_preprocessor(binary=BINARY):
    """Build the preprocessing step. `binary` lets us drop a binary feature."""
    return make_column_transformer(
        (make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler()), NUMERIC),
        (
            make_pipeline(
                SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="Unknown"),
                OneHotEncoder(
                    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
                    min_frequency=MIN_CATEGORY_COUNT,
                    sparse_output=False,
                ),
            ),
            CATEGORICAL,
        ),
        (OneHotEncoder(drop="if_binary", sparse_output=False), binary),
    )
```

As a baseline, we used a dummy classifier that ignores the predictors and always predicts the most common outcome in the training folds. Any useful model should do clearly better than this baseline.

```{python}
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

dummy_cv = cross_validate(
    make_pipeline(make_preprocessor(), DummyClassifier()),
    X_train,
    y_train,
    groups=groups_train,
    cv=cv,
    scoring="balanced_accuracy",
)
dummy_score = dummy_cv["test_score"].mean()
```

Our first model was logistic regression. It is a natural starting point for a binary outcome: it is fast to fit, and its coefficients show which features are linked to a higher or lower chance of summiting, which matters for a question about planning decisions. Its main hyperparameter, C, controls the strength of regularisation, with smaller values shrinking the coefficients more strongly towards zero. We tuned C over six values from 0.001 to 100 on a logarithmic grid, using grouped cross-validation on the training set.

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

C_GRID = np.logspace(-3, 2, 6)


def tune_logistic_regression(features, binary):
    search = GridSearchCV(
        make_pipeline(make_preprocessor(binary), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
        {"logisticregression__C": C_GRID},
        cv=cv,
        scoring="balanced_accuracy",
        n_jobs=-1,
    )
    search.fit(train_df[features], y_train, groups=groups_train)
    return search


lr_search = tune_logistic_regression(NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL + BINARY, BINARY)
lr_score = lr_search.best_score_
best_c = lr_search.best_params_["logisticregression__C"]

lr_scores = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "C": lr_search.cv_results_["param_logisticregression__C"].astype(float),
        "score": lr_search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"],
        "sd": lr_search.cv_results_["std_test_score"],
    }
)
smallest_good_c = lr_scores.loc[lr_scores["score"] >= lr_score - 0.005, "C"].min()

dummy_str = f"{dummy_score:.2f}"
lr_str = f"{lr_score:.3f}"
best_c_str = f"{best_c:g}"
smallest_good_c_str = f"{smallest_good_c:g}"
```

@fig-lr-tuning shows the cross-validation score for each value of C. The best value was C = `{python} best_c_str`, with a mean balanced accuracy of `{python} lr_str`, compared with `{python} dummy_str` for the dummy baseline. The score is almost flat from C = `{python} smallest_good_c_str` upwards (within 0.005 of the best score), so the model is not sensitive to the exact choice of C as long as the regularisation is not too strong.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lr-tuning
#| fig-cap: "Mean cross-validation balanced accuracy of logistic regression for each value of the regularisation hyperparameter C. The shaded band is plus or minus one standard deviation across the five folds. The dashed line is the dummy baseline."
lr_band = alt.Chart(lr_scores).transform_calculate(
    lower="datum.score - datum.sd", upper="datum.score + datum.sd"
).mark_area(opacity=0.2, color="#7570b3").encode(
    x=alt.X("C:Q", scale=alt.Scale(type="log")),
    y="lower:Q",
    y2="upper:Q",
)
lr_line = alt.Chart(lr_scores).mark_line(point=True, color="#7570b3").encode(
    x=alt.X(
        "C:Q",
        title="Regularisation hyperparameter C (log scale)",
        scale=alt.Scale(type="log"),
    ),
    y=alt.Y(
        "score:Q",
        title="Mean CV balanced accuracy",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0.45, 0.75]),
    ),
    tooltip=[alt.Tooltip("C:Q", format="g"), alt.Tooltip("score:Q", format=".3f")],
)
dummy_rule = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({"score": [dummy_score]})).mark_rule(
    strokeDash=[4, 4], color="black"
).encode(y="score:Q")

(lr_band + lr_line + dummy_rule).properties(width=450, height=250)
```

Logistic regression assumes that each feature changes the log-odds of summiting by a fixed amount, regardless of the other features. The exploratory analysis suggested that this may be too simple: for example, the benefit of hired support or oxygen may depend on how high the peak is. Our second model was therefore a histogram-based gradient boosting classifier, which builds an ensemble of decision trees, each correcting the errors of the previous ones. Tree ensembles can capture non-linear effects and interactions between features without us having to specify them, and the histogram-based implementation is fast on a data set of this size. It used the same preprocessing pipeline as logistic regression.

We tuned three hyperparameters: the maximum depth of each tree, which controls how complex the interactions can be; the number of boosting iterations, that is, the number of trees; and the learning rate, which controls how much each tree contributes. Because there are three hyperparameters, we used a randomised search over 20 combinations rather than a full grid, again with grouped 5-fold cross-validation and balanced accuracy.

```{python}
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV

hgb_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    make_pipeline(make_preprocessor(), HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=522)),
    {
        "histgradientboostingclassifier__max_depth": [3, 5, 8, None],
        "histgradientboostingclassifier__max_iter": randint(100, 500),
        "histgradientboostingclassifier__learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.3),
    },
    n_iter=20,
    cv=cv,
    scoring="balanced_accuracy",
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=522,
)
hgb_search.fit(X_train, y_train, groups=groups_train)
hgb_score = hgb_search.best_score_

hgb_best = hgb_search.best_params_
hgb_depth = hgb_best["histgradientboostingclassifier__max_depth"]
hgb_depth_str = (
    "no limit on tree depth (each tree is still limited to 31 leaves by default)"
    if hgb_depth is None
    else f"a maximum tree depth of {hgb_depth}"
)
hgb_iter_str = str(hgb_best["histgradientboostingclassifier__max_iter"])
hgb_lr_str = f"{hgb_best['histgradientboostingclassifier__learning_rate']:.3f}"
hgb_str = f"{hgb_score:.3f}"
```

The best combination used `{python} hgb_depth_str`, `{python} hgb_iter_str` trees and a learning rate of `{python} hgb_lr_str`, with a mean cross-validation balanced accuracy of `{python} hgb_str`.

## Results

### What the logistic regression learned

```{python}
FEATURE_TITLES = {
    "year": "Year",
    "age": "Age",
    "team_size": "Team size",
    "hired_staff": "Number of hired staff",
    "peak_height_m": "Peak height",
    "season": "Season",
    "sex": "Sex",
    "citizenship": "Citizenship",
    "expedition_role": "Expedition role",
    "hired": "Hired staff",
    "solo": "Solo climb",
    "expedition_oxygen": "Expedition used oxygen",
}
LEVEL_LABELS = {
    "BC Manager": "base camp manager",
    "H-A Worker": "high-altitude worker",
    "H-A Assistant": "high-altitude assistant",
    "Exp Doctor": "expedition doctor",
    "Sirdar": "sirdar (head of the hired staff)",
    "S Korea": "South Korea",
    "S Africa": "South Africa",
    "F": "female",
    "M": "male",
    "infrequent_sklearn": "other (rare levels)",
}


def readable_name(feature_name):
    """Turn a name such as 'pipeline-2__season_Summer' into 'Season: Summer'."""
    column_part = feature_name.split("__", 1)[1]
    for column, title in FEATURE_TITLES.items():
        if column_part in (column, f"{column}_True"):
            return title
        if column_part.startswith(f"{column}_"):
            level = column_part[len(column) + 1:]
            return f"{title}: {LEVEL_LABELS.get(level, level)}"
    return column_part


best_lr = lr_search.best_estimator_
coefficients = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Feature": [readable_name(n) for n in best_lr[0].get_feature_names_out()],
        "Coefficient": best_lr[-1].coef_[0],
    }
)
coef_lookup = coefficients.set_index("Feature")["Coefficient"]
top_coefficients = (
    coefficients.reindex(coefficients["Coefficient"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
    .head(10)
    .assign(**{"Effect on chance of summiting": lambda d: np.where(d["Coefficient"] > 0, "Higher", "Lower")})
)

bc_coef_str = f"{coef_lookup['Expedition role: base camp manager']:.1f}"
oxygen_coef_str = f"{coef_lookup['Expedition used oxygen']:.1f}"
solo_coef_str = f"{coef_lookup['Solo climb']:.1f}"
n_solo_str = f"{train_df['solo'].sum():,}"
sex_gap_str = f"{abs(coef_lookup['Sex: male'] - coef_lookup['Sex: female']):.2f}"
```

@tbl-coefs lists the ten features with the largest coefficients in the best logistic regression model, fitted on the whole training set. Numeric features were standardised, so their coefficients describe the change in the log-odds of summiting for a one standard deviation increase. Each level of a categorical feature has its own coefficient, which is best read relative to the other levels of the same feature.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "The ten largest logistic regression coefficients by absolute value. Positive coefficients are linked to a higher chance of reaching the summit and negative coefficients to a lower chance."
top_coefficients.style.hide(axis="index").format({"Coefficient": "{:.2f}"})
```

The largest coefficient by far belongs to base camp managers (`{python} bc_coef_str`). None of the base camp managers in the training set reached the summit, which is expected because their job is to run base camp rather than to climb. This shows that the expedition role partly encodes whether a member intended to go to the summit at all. Expedition oxygen use has the largest positive coefficient (`{python} oxygen_coef_str`), in line with the exploratory analysis. Solo climbing also has a large positive coefficient (`{python} solo_coef_str`), but only `{python} n_solo_str` training members climbed solo, so this estimate is very uncertain. Leadership roles were linked to a higher chance of summiting than ordinary climbers, and climbing in summer to a lower chance than the other seasons. In contrast, the coefficients for female and male members differ by only `{python} sex_gap_str`, so once the other features are taken into account, sex adds little to the prediction, even though men summited somewhat more often overall (@fig-categorical).

### The role of expedition oxygen use

As noted in the exploratory analysis, the expedition-level oxygen indicator may be partly recorded after the climb, since an expedition that turned back early might never use the oxygen it planned to use. To see how much the model depends on it, we tuned a second logistic regression in the same way but without this feature.

```{python}
lr_no_oxygen_search = tune_logistic_regression(
    NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL + ["hired", "solo"], ["hired", "solo"]
)
lr_no_oxygen_score = lr_no_oxygen_search.best_score_

lr_no_oxygen_str = f"{lr_no_oxygen_score:.3f}"
# Use the rounded scores so the drop matches the numbers shown in the text
oxygen_drop_str = f"{round(lr_score, 3) - round(lr_no_oxygen_score, 3):.3f}"
```

Without expedition oxygen use, the best cross-validation balanced accuracy fell from `{python} lr_str` to `{python} lr_no_oxygen_str`, a drop of `{python} oxygen_drop_str`. The model therefore still predicts clearly better than the dummy baseline (`{python} dummy_str`) without this feature, but oxygen use accounts for a noticeable part of its performance. If the indicator does partly reflect what happened during the climb, the scores of the models that use it are somewhat optimistic. We keep the feature in the main models because planned oxygen use is genuinely known before an expedition sets off, and we return to this limitation in the Discussion.

### Model comparison

```{python}
def best_cv_sd(search):
    return search.cv_results_["std_test_score"][search.best_index_]


model_comparison = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Model": [
            "Dummy baseline (most frequent class)",
            "Logistic regression without expedition oxygen",
            "Logistic regression",
            "Gradient boosting",
        ],
        "Mean CV balanced accuracy": [
            dummy_score,
            lr_no_oxygen_score,
            lr_score,
            hgb_score,
        ],
        "SD across folds": [
            dummy_cv["test_score"].std(),
            best_cv_sd(lr_no_oxygen_search),
            best_cv_sd(lr_search),
            best_cv_sd(hgb_search),
        ],
    }
)

hgb_gain_str = f"{round(hgb_score, 3) - round(lr_score, 3):.3f}"
max_sd_str = f"{model_comparison['SD across folds'].iloc[1:].max():.3f}"
```

@tbl-model-comparison summarises the cross-validation results. Both logistic regression models are far better than the dummy baseline. Gradient boosting reached a mean balanced accuracy of `{python} hgb_str`, `{python} hgb_gain_str` higher than logistic regression. This gain is larger than the variation between folds (standard deviations of at most `{python} max_sd_str` for the three real models), which suggests that the interactions and non-linear effects captured by the trees do carry real information about summit success. We therefore chose gradient boosting as our final model.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and standard deviation (SD) of balanced accuracy across the five grouped cross-validation folds on the training set, for each model with its best hyperparameters."
model_comparison.style.hide(axis="index").format(
    {"Mean CV balanced accuracy": "{:.3f}", "SD across folds": "{:.3f}"}
)
```

### Performance on the test set

Up to this point, every decision was made using the training set only. We then evaluated the final gradient boosting model, refitted on the whole training set with its best hyperparameters, once on the test set.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score, confusion_matrix

final_model = hgb_search.best_estimator_
X_test = test_df[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL + BINARY]
y_test = test_df["success"]
y_pred = final_model.predict(X_test)

test_score = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=[False, True]).ravel()
summit_recall = tp / (tp + fn)
no_summit_recall = tn / (tn + fp)
summit_precision = tp / (tp + fp)

test_str = f"{test_score:.3f}"
n_test_str = f"{len(test_df):,}"
n_test_exp_str = f"{test_df['expedition_id'].nunique():,}"
summit_recall_str = f"{summit_recall:.0%}"
no_summit_recall_str = f"{no_summit_recall:.0%}"
summit_precision_str = f"{summit_precision:.0%}"
no_summit_precision_str = f"{tn / (tn + fn):.0%}"
fn_str = f"{fn:,}"
fp_str = f"{fp:,}"
```

On the `{python} n_test_str` test members from `{python} n_test_exp_str` expeditions, none of which were seen during training, the final model reached a balanced accuracy of `{python} test_str`. This is slightly lower than its cross-validation score of `{python} hgb_str`. A small drop is expected, because the hyperparameters were chosen as the best of 20 combinations on the same cross-validation folds, which makes the best cross-validation score a little optimistic. The model still performs well above the dummy baseline on expeditions it has never seen.

@fig-confusion shows the test set predictions in more detail. The model correctly identified `{python} summit_recall_str` of the members who reached the summit and `{python} no_summit_recall_str` of those who did not. When it predicted that a member would summit, it was right `{python} summit_precision_str` of the time. The model is therefore somewhat cautious: it missed `{python} fn_str` members who did reach the summit, compared with `{python} fp_str` members who were wrongly predicted to succeed. When it predicted that a member would not summit, it was right `{python} no_summit_precision_str` of the time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-confusion
#| fig-cap: "Confusion matrix of the final gradient boosting model on the test set. Each cell shows the number of test members with that combination of actual and predicted outcome."
confusion = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Actual outcome": ["Did not summit", "Did not summit", "Summited", "Summited"],
        "Predicted outcome": ["Did not summit", "Summited", "Did not summit", "Summited"],
        "Members": [tn, fp, fn, tp],
    }
)
outcome_order = ["Summited", "Did not summit"]
confusion_base = alt.Chart(confusion).encode(
    x=alt.X("Predicted outcome:N", sort=outcome_order, axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
    y=alt.Y("Actual outcome:N", sort=outcome_order),
)
confusion_cells = confusion_base.mark_rect().encode(
    color=alt.Color("Members:Q", scale=alt.Scale(scheme="purples"), legend=None),
    tooltip=["Actual outcome", "Predicted outcome", alt.Tooltip("Members:Q", format=",")],
)
confusion_text = confusion_base.mark_text(fontSize=16).encode(
    text=alt.Text("Members:Q", format=","),
    color=alt.condition(
        alt.datum.Members > confusion["Members"].max() / 2,
        alt.value("white"),
        alt.value("black"),
    ),
)
(confusion_cells + confusion_text).properties(width=300, height=220)
```

## Discussion

We asked whether information known before an expedition begins can predict whether an individual member will reach the summit. The answer is a qualified yes. Our final gradient boosting model reached a balanced accuracy of `{python} test_str` on expeditions it had never seen, well above the `{python} dummy_str` of a baseline that ignores the predictors. Pre-expedition information therefore carries real signal about summit success. At the same time, the model misclassified a substantial share of members in both outcome groups (@fig-confusion), so this information is far from enough to determine who will reach the top.

In the context of Himalayan climbing, this is a reasonable result. Whether a climber summits also depends on weather, route conditions, illness, fitness on the day and decisions made high on the mountain, none of which can be known in advance or are recorded in our data. What the model does show is which planning factors are most strongly linked to success. Hired status and expedition oxygen use stood out in the exploratory analysis (@fig-categorical), and expedition role and oxygen use had the largest logistic regression coefficients (@tbl-coefs). Gradient boosting improved on logistic regression (@tbl-model-comparison), which suggests that the effects of these factors depend on each other and on the peak, rather than adding up independently.

Many of these patterns are what we expected. Hired staff and expeditions that use supplemental oxygen are central to commercial climbing on the highest peaks, and we expected them to be linked to success. The higher success rates of younger members and of more recent years in our exploratory analysis (@fig-numeric) are consistent with earlier work on Everest, which found that success rates roughly doubled between 1990-2005 and 2006-2019 and that success declines with age after about 40 (Huey et al. 2020). The same study found nearly identical success rates for women and men on Everest, which agrees with our finding that sex adds little to the prediction once the other features are taken into account. We were more surprised that peak height on its own separated the outcomes so poorly, and that peaks of almost the same height had very different success rates (@fig-peaks). This points to route difficulty and the level of commercial support on each peak as important factors that our features capture only indirectly.

Our findings have several limitations:

- **Expedition oxygen use.** The expedition-level oxygen indicator may be partly recorded after the climb. Without it, the cross-validation balanced accuracy of logistic regression fell from `{python} lr_str` to `{python} lr_no_oxygen_str`, so our reported performance is likely somewhat optimistic.
- **Expedition role.** The role partly records whether a member planned to go to the summit at all. For example, no base camp manager in the training set summited. Part of the model's performance comes from recognising these roles rather than from predicting the outcome of an attempt.
- **Data coverage.** The data end in spring 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic and before recent changes in commercial climbing. The records are also compiled from reports by expeditions, so some details may be missing or inaccurate.
- **Unbalanced peaks.** A few popular peaks make up most of the data, with Everest alone accounting for about a third of members. The model may perform worse on rarely climbed peaks, which we did not evaluate separately.
- **Missing climber information.** Important factors such as previous climbing experience and fitness are not in the data. Citizenship may act as a rough stand-in for experience, wealth or access to guided expeditions, so its coefficients should not be read as an effect of nationality itself.

If developed further, a model like this could help climbers and expedition organisers set realistic expectations and see which planning choices are linked to better outcomes. It should not be used to judge individual climbers, and certainly not to decide who receives a climbing permit. Its predictions are uncertain for any single person, and features such as citizenship and sex could lead to unfair decisions if used in that way.

This analysis leads to several further questions. Would adding peak identity or route, or each climber's previous expeditions, improve predictions substantially? How well does the model perform when it is restricted to members who intended to reach the summit, which would remove the shortcut provided by roles such as base camp manager? Does performance differ between popular and rarely climbed peaks? Finally, the same approach could be used to study an outcome that matters even more for safety: the risk of death or serious injury.
